404.html: Not found That page is not part of this site. Start from the map , or look a term up in the terminology . AI SDLC The software development lifecycle (SDLC) with AI agents doing part of the work in every phase, from intent and specification through design, build, verification, release and operation, while deterministic checks and human decisions stay where they are needed. Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. It cannot change the evidence schema, redefine a result state or waive a rule the core marks as never open to exception. coined Golden path The opinionated, supported way to build a kind of system that a platform offers its users, with templates and documentation, so that each team does not assemble its own tooling. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. On this site, an architecture rule expressed as a fitness function that runs with the build is a validator, and an architecture gate once it blocks. adopted ford-evolutionary-architectures Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a verify command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a few validators for rules the team has broken before, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency rules, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. It proposes; it cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Flexible and scalable, but itself non-deterministic and subject to position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so its grades are checked against human judgement before they are relied on. In an eval set it is one kind of grader, alongside code-based checks and human review. adopted zheng-llm-judge Evidence record What a run records in one fixed shape, as a by-product of the run rather than a report written afterwards: schema version, change and configuration revisions, kit version, the checks expected before the run, each check's result with its rule ID, status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending and taken, and an overall status derived from the rest. Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable), it timed out again after one retry, or the tool itself crashed. It is never reported as passed or skipped; what it means for a merge or release is decided in assurance. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. The name is this site's; the distinction is established, for example in SARIF's record of whether a tool's execution succeeded, and in test frameworks that report errors apart from failures. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives), a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended), a work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. It translates; it holds no rules, validator logic or schema. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. Adapted from Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters pattern (see that entry): his adapters sit at an application's ports, and this site applies the idea to the one layer of a kit that talks to outside tools. adapted cockburn-hexagonal Ports and adapters Alistair Cockburn's architecture pattern, also called hexagonal architecture: an application talks to the outside world only through ports, and a technology-specific adapter at each port translates between the outside device and the application, so the application can be driven by people, programs or tests and developed apart from the devices and databases it runs against. The Engineering Kit's tool adapters apply the same idea to the tools a kit runs against. adopted cockburn-hexagonal Anticorruption layer Eric Evans's domain-driven design pattern: an isolating layer that talks to another system through its existing interface and translates between the two models, so the other system's concepts do not reshape the model that uses it. A kit's adapters play this part between the kit's core and a tool's own vocabulary. adopted evans-ddd-reference Contract test Martin Fowler's name for a test that checks a test double still behaves like the real outside service it stands in for. It runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes. On this site, the contract suite a kit's core defines for each kind of adapter is the same idea pointed at the kit's own interface. adopted fowler-contract-test Consumer-driven contract Ian Robinson's service-evolution pattern: the consumers of a service state their expectations as tests, and the provider is checked against all of them, so it can change without breaking any consumer. adopted robinson-cdc Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. The idea of scaling test effort to risk comes from risk-based testing. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating state that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. Coined in this sense. Earlier uses of the phrase mean something else: Cusumano (1991) for Japanese firms that applied production-management discipline to large-scale software development, and Greenfield and Short (2004) for model-driven production of variants of a standard product. Recent writing on the "dark software factory", where agents produce software that no person reviews, is not what is meant either, nor is the industrial sense of identical outputs from a fixed process. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, plan and tasks, with clarification added where the specification leaves questions open. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. coined Independent basis for verification If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. The law does not say fewer controls are better. This site's recommendation follows from shrinking what is governed: narrow what the agent may produce first, on a few well-defined execution surfaces, then start with a small set of controls fitted to failures actually seen. adopted ashby
adapters.html: Adapters The thin layer that binds an Engineering Kit's core to each tool it runs against, so that its rules, validators and evidence schema depend on no one product. Definition An adapter is the thin binding between an Engineering Kit 's core and one tool the kit runs against: the execution surface where the coding agent works, the change host where the pull request lives, the pipeline runner where checks run unattended, the work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. The core holds what the team means: its rules, its validators and its evidence schema. The adapter holds only what it takes to talk to one product. The idea comes from Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters pattern, also called hexagonal architecture, in which a technology-specific adapter turns whatever arrives at a port into a call the application understands, so the application does not depend on the device on the other side 3 . Using "adapter" as the name of one layer of a kit is this site's own usage. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. Why it matters In an AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), the same checks have to run wherever the work happens: on a developer's machine, inside the agent's execution surface, and in the pipeline that guards the merge. A kit that calls one product's interface from inside its rules is tied to that product's release cycle and vocabulary. When the product changes its interface, or the team moves to another, the rules have to be rewritten, and results differ between environments while that work is under way. Cockburn's motivating problem applies directly. A layer that is promised to hold no business logic, with nothing in place to detect a breach of that promise, collects business logic over the years, and logic in the wrong layer can no longer be exercised by automated test suites 3 . Domain-driven design describes the same risk between models: without an isolating layer, another system's model can gradually reshape the model that uses it. Eric Evans's anticorruption layer talks to the other system through its existing interface and translates in both directions, so the other system's concepts stay outside 4 . For a kit, the outside model is a tool's own idea of a check, a status, a work item or a permission. A tool-free core also keeps the harness portable. The tools an agent can call are part of its harness 1 , and a team's choice of tools changes over time. A kit whose meaning sits in the core follows those changes by swapping bindings, not by re-deriving its rules. The Twelve-Factor App makes the parallel point about backing services: code that treats each outside service as an attached resource can exchange one for another through configuration, without code changes 17 . How it works The bindings a kit needs No public source lists the bindings an agent engineering kit needs; the list below is recommended practice. A kit ships one adapter per tool the team uses, not a fixed set. Execution surface. Installs the kit's guidance and commands in the form the surface loads, and lets the agent run the same verify command a person runs. Change host. Reads the change and its metadata, posts each result as a check on the pull request, and links the report behind it. Pipeline runner. Runs the kit's commands unattended, with the same inputs as a local run, and collects the evidence record the run produces. Work tracker. Reads and writes the few work-item fields the kit relies on, such as the link between a change and the item it serves. Tool servers. Connect the agent to capabilities published over an interface. The Model Context Protocol is one example: an open protocol in which servers offer tools, resources and prompts to client applications using JSON-RPC 2.0 messages 10 . An HTTP API described in the OpenAPI Specification, a language-agnostic description of what a service offers, is another 12 . What goes in an adapter, and what stays in the core The split follows the difference between mechanism and meaning. It is recommended practice, resting by analogy on Cockburn's and Evans's patterns. Stays in the core Goes in an adapter Rule identifiers, routes and owners (the rule registry ) Endpoints, authentication calls and rate-limit handling Validator logic and the results it returns Translating the tool's input into the core's interface The evidence schema and what each field means Translating the core's results into the tool's vocabulary: a check, a status, a comment The four results a check can report: passed, failed, skipped and could_not_run Packaging the kit in the form the tool loads Validators are deterministic checks of the kind Birgitta Böckeler calls computational sensors 2 , and they belong in the core. The adapter passes on what validators return and adds no verdict of its own. It also does not restate a machine-checkable rule as text for a model to read, since only the validator gives the same answer on every run. Once a rule lives in a binding, replacing the tool means rewriting the rule. The boundary is enforced by a check, not by a convention. An architecture rule can be written as an executable test 5 , for example a test that fails when any module in the core imports from an adapter. One model vendor's account of harness engineering describes enforcing architectural constraints through automated checks in the same way 11 . Cockburn's observation that an unguarded boundary erodes is the reason for making it a check. Every adapter follows an interface that its owners do not control and has to keep up with it, so, as recommended practice, a team writes one only for a tool it actually uses and only where configuration cannot express the need. An integration the tool's users already publish can serve as the adapter, provided it passes the same contract suite as one the team writes itself. How an adapter is tested Testing follows the same split. The recommended practice below builds on two public patterns. Ian Robinson's consumer-driven contracts have each consumer of a service state its expectations as tests that the provider runs, so the provider can change without breaking any of its consumers 13 . Martin Fowler's contract test checks that a test double still answers the way the real outside service does; it runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes, and a failure starts work to bring the two back into line rather than necessarily breaking the build 7 . Applied to a kit: One contract suite per binding. The core states what it expects of any change-host adapter, any pipeline-runner adapter and so on, as tests against the core's interface. Every adapter for that binding must pass the same suite. A double in the fast checks, the real tool in the contract run. Checks on the adapter's own changes use a double of the tool, so they stay quick and repeatable. The contract run against the real tool happens separately, as Fowler describes, and shows when the double has stopped matching. The tool's own failures. The suite includes runs in which the tool is unreachable or answers with an error, and the adapter must report could_not_run with that cause, never failed and never passed. A code-coverage target set for the core fits an adapter poorly. Most of an adapter's lines call a tool that the fast checks replace with a double, so a high percentage there mostly measures the double. The measure for an adapter is whether it passes its binding's contract suite, failure runs included. An adapter that needs many tests of its own to reach a target has usually taken on logic that belongs in the core. This is recommended practice. The same result locally and in CI Continuous integration expects anyone to be able to check out the sources on a clean machine and build and test the system with one command, and the same build to run after every push to the mainline 6 . The Thoughtworks Technology Radar places pipeline configuration treated as code, kept under source control and tested like any other code, in its Adopt ring 16 . For a kit, the pipeline-runner adapter calls the same verify a developer runs. It adds scheduling and reporting, never extra checks or different thresholds, so a difference between a local result and a pipeline result points at the environment, not at the rules. Adapters do not remove every difference: the Twelve-Factor App warns that even when adapters appear to hide the differences between backing services, small incompatibilities let code pass in one environment and fail in another 18 . That is why the contract run against the real tool stays. Versions, replacement and synchronisation An adapter is versioned and released separately from the core, and states the range of core versions it works with. Semantic Versioning makes such a range readable, because a new major version marks an incompatible change to a declared public interface 14 . When the core or the tool changes its interface, the contract suite shows whether the adapter still holds. Replacing a tool means writing a new adapter, passing the same contract suite, and switching. Rules, validators and schema stay as they are; that is the design intent of the layer, not a measured result. An adapter that keeps two systems in step, such as the repository and the work tracker, first settles which system owns each field and copies that field in one direction only. Where a field can still be edited in both places, a clash goes to a person rather than being settled automatically, because keeping whichever edit is newer silently throws the other one away. This is recommended practice. Reporting that a tool could not run Test frameworks already keep "could not run here" apart from "failed": in one widely used framework, a test whose assumption about the runtime environment does not hold is aborted rather than failed. 9 Change hosts, however, have their own list of check states, and the adapter has to choose one. It never chooses success, and it avoids any state the host treats as satisfying a required check: at least one change host accepts a skipped or neutral required check as passing. 8 So, as recommended practice, the adapter posts could_not_run in a state that is not successful, names the cause in the check's summary, and links the evidence. What that state means for the merge is decided in the assurance band of the map. On the pull request, the change-host adapter posts each check's result, with a link to that check's evidence, and alongside them the overall status that the evidence record carries. The adapter computes neither: validators produce the results and the evidence record derives the overall status. A check new to the team is posted as report-only at first, so its results are visible without holding changes, and is marked required later. The adapter posts the same result in both stages; only the label the change host attaches to it differs. The running example The customer-record export arrives as a pull request. The pipeline-runner adapter runs verify unattended, and gets the same result a developer gets locally: the validator for R-042, the access rule on which identities may export which records, fails because a background worker queries more records than the requesting user may see. The change-host adapter posts that failure as a check on the pull request and links the validator's report. The runner image lacks the load-test tool, so the 50k-row load scenario for R-017, the volume-limit rule, cannot start. The adapter posts that check as not successful, with could_not_run and the missing tool as its cause, rather than dropping it or showing it as passed, and posts the record's overall status of blocked beside the two checks. If the team later moves to another change host, only the change-host adapter is rewritten and passed through the same contract suite. R-042, R-017, their validators and the evidence schema do not change. Where it sits on the map Adapters sit in the core band, the part of the map that does the work, inside the Engineering Kit box as one of its five parts alongside the rule registry, validators, skills with evals and the evidence schema. Within the kit's four layers (shared core, technology profiles , tool adapters and project configuration ), adapters are the layer that faces outward. On one side are the rules, validators and schema they carry without changing. On the other side are the tools themselves, the execution surface, change host, pipeline runner, work tracker and tool servers, whose choice and configuration belong to the enablement band. So do the permissions and secrets an adapter uses, which follow the usual rule for automation: each automated actor has its own machine identity with no more access than its job needs. Adapters also carry the evidence record to the pull request, where a workflow 's human decision is taken, and the assurance band reads the same results to decide whether a change may merge or release. Pitfalls Rules in the binding. A rule or threshold is written into an adapter, and replacing the tool would change what is enforced. Sign: a rule change needs an adapter edit, or two adapters give different results for the same change. An adapter that grows a validator. The adapter starts to judge the product instead of translating. Sign: the adapter has tests about product behaviour, or it becomes the subject of coverage arguments. A lowest-common-denominator core. The core's interface is cut down to what every tool supports. Thoughtworks places generic cloud usage on Hold for the same reason in a different setting: avoiding lock-in at all costs gives up each provider's distinctive benefits 15 . The comparison is an analogy. Sign: a core capability waits for the least capable tool. Absence read as a pass. A tool is missing and the check quietly disappears. Sign: a check vanishes from the pull request after a runner image change, or skipped results rise with no stated cause. Local and pipeline results drift apart. The pipeline defines steps of its own. Sign: changes pass locally and fail in the pipeline with no code difference. Doubles that no longer match the tool. The contract suite runs only against doubles. Sign: the first sign of a tool's interface change is a failure reported by users. Silent upgrades. An adapter says nothing about which core versions it works with. Sign: it breaks after an upgrade on either side and nobody is sure who fixes it. A sync adapter that settles clashes by itself. Conflicting edits are resolved by whichever came last. Sign: a value in the tracker changes and nobody reviewed the change. The same fix copied from project to project. Each project patches its tool binding for itself. Sign: several near-identical patches, no two quite the same, and no agreed version. Related Engineering Kit : the package adapters belong to, its layers and its commands. Validators : the deterministic checks adapters run and report, including how a validator reports that it could not run. Evidence schema : the fixed shape of the record adapters carry to the change host, including the overall status it derives. Rule registry : the identifiers adapters pass through unchanged. Workflows : the unit of work whose checks and decisions adapters connect to real tools. Harness engineering : the discipline the kit and its adapters serve. Terminology: adapter and the workflow catalog . Sources The adapter idea is Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters pattern 3 , with Eric Evans's anticorruption layer as the related domain-driven design pattern 4 . The place of tools in the harness follows Birgitta Böckeler 1 , and validators as computational sensors follow her worked examples 2 . Testing draws on Ian Robinson's consumer-driven contracts 13 and Martin Fowler's contract test 7 ; local and pipeline parity on Fowler's account of continuous integration 6 , the Thoughtworks Technology Radar on pipelines as code 16 and the Twelve-Factor App on parity and backing services 18 17 . Enforcing the boundary draws on fitness functions 5 and one model vendor's account of harness engineering 11 . Version ranges follow Semantic Versioning 14 . Tool-server interfaces cite their own specifications 10 12 ; the aborted-versus-failed precedent cites its framework's documentation 9 ; the behaviour of skipped required checks cites one change host's documentation 8 ; the lock-in analogy cites the Radar 15 . The list of bindings, the split between core and adapter, the contract-suite approach in place of coverage targets, one-way field ownership in synchronisation and reporting could_not_run through the change host are recommended practice with no public source that states them for kits.
