analyzers around 10% are put on probation. ↩ ↩ Lightweight Architecture Decision Records — Thoughtworks, Thoughtworks Technology Radar, Volume 17 (archived entry) — 2017-11 (Adopt) · source Radar technique in the Adopt ring recommending that architecture decision records, with their context and consequences, be kept in source control alongside the code rather than in a wiki. ↩ ↩ Security policy as code — Thoughtworks, Thoughtworks Technology Radar, Volume 23 (archived entry) — 2020-10 (Trial) · source Radar technique describing security policies written as files under version control, validated automatically in the pipeline, deployed automatically and monitored. ↩ ↩ AI SDLC The software development lifecycle (SDLC) with AI agents doing part of the work in every phase, from intent and specification through design, build, verification, release and operation, while deterministic checks and human decisions stay where they are needed. Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. It cannot change the evidence schema, redefine a result state or waive a rule the core marks as never open to exception. coined Golden path The opinionated, supported way to build a kind of system that a platform offers its users, with templates and documentation, so that each team does not assemble its own tooling. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. On this site, an architecture rule expressed as a fitness function that runs with the build is a validator, and an architecture gate once it blocks. adopted ford-evolutionary-architectures Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a verify command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a few validators for rules the team has broken before, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency rules, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. It proposes; it cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Flexible and scalable, but itself non-deterministic and subject to position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so its grades are checked against human judgement before they are relied on. In an eval set it is one kind of grader, alongside code-based checks and human review. adopted zheng-llm-judge Evidence record What a run records in one fixed shape, as a by-product of the run rather than a report written afterwards: schema version, change and configuration revisions, kit version, the checks expected before the run, each check's result with its rule ID, status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending and taken, and an overall status derived from the rest. Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable), it timed out again after one retry, or the tool itself crashed. It is never reported as passed or skipped; what it means for a merge or release is decided in assurance. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. The name is this site's; the distinction is established, for example in SARIF's record of whether a tool's execution succeeded, and in test frameworks that report errors apart from failures. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives), a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended), a work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. It translates; it holds no rules, validator logic or schema. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. Adapted from Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters pattern (see that entry): his adapters sit at an application's ports, and this site applies the idea to the one layer of a kit that talks to outside tools. adapted cockburn-hexagonal Ports and adapters Alistair Cockburn's architecture pattern, also called hexagonal architecture: an application talks to the outside world only through ports, and a technology-specific adapter at each port translates between the outside device and the application, so the application can be driven by people, programs or tests and developed apart from the devices and databases it runs against. The Engineering Kit's tool adapters apply the same idea to the tools a kit runs against. adopted cockburn-hexagonal Anticorruption layer Eric Evans's domain-driven design pattern: an isolating layer that talks to another system through its existing interface and translates between the two models, so the other system's concepts do not reshape the model that uses it. A kit's adapters play this part between the kit's core and a tool's own vocabulary. adopted evans-ddd-reference Contract test Martin Fowler's name for a test that checks a test double still behaves like the real outside service it stands in for. It runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes. On this site, the contract suite a kit's core defines for each kind of adapter is the same idea pointed at the kit's own interface. adopted fowler-contract-test Consumer-driven contract Ian Robinson's service-evolution pattern: the consumers of a service state their expectations as tests, and the provider is checked against all of them, so it can change without breaking any consumer. adopted robinson-cdc Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. The idea of scaling test effort to risk comes from risk-based testing. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating state that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. Coined in this sense. Earlier uses of the phrase mean something else: Cusumano (1991) for Japanese firms that applied production-management discipline to large-scale software development, and Greenfield and Short (2004) for model-driven production of variants of a standard product. Recent writing on the "dark software factory", where agents produce software that no person reviews, is not what is meant either, nor is the industrial sense of identical outputs from a fixed process. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, plan and tasks, with clarification added where the specification leaves questions open. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. coined Independent basis for verification If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. The law does not say fewer controls are better. This site's recommendation follows from shrinking what is governed: narrow what the agent may produce first, on a few well-defined execution surfaces, then start with a small set of controls fitted to failures actually seen. adopted ashby
skills-and-evals.html: Skills with evals A skill is packaged guidance a coding agent loads when a task calls for it; because it shapes behaviour without guaranteeing it, it ships with a record of scenario evaluations rather than on one passing run. Definition A skill is a packaged piece of guidance that a coding agent loads only when the task in hand calls for it: a short name and description the agent scans, a body of instructions it reads once it decides the skill applies, and, optionally, scripts and reference files it can use along the way. 4 3 The folder-and-file format is published as an open specification that a range of AI systems use. 8 3 In Birgitta Böckeler's vocabulary a skill is a guide, a control that steers the agent before it acts, as opposed to a sensor, which observes the result afterwards. 5 On this site a skill also names the rules it supports, and it ships with evals: a set of scenarios that test whether an agent working with the skill behaves as intended, run repeatedly and recorded across versions. A review skill is the sensor counterpart. It reads a change against the applicable rules and reports findings, which is what Böckeler calls an inferential sensor. 6 Why it matters In an AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), much of what a team knows about doing the work well has to reach the agent somehow: which records an export may return, which fields never leave the system, when to stop and ask. Written once as a skill, that know-how reaches every task that needs it without filling the agent's context on tasks that do not. 4 The risk is that a team starts treating the skill as a guarantee. Böckeler warns that as long as a language model is involved, the outcome remains a matter of probability. 4 One vendor's skill-authoring guidance uses exactly that failure as its worked example: an agent writes a query and leaves out a filter that the loaded skill tells it to apply. 7 The same prompt can also produce different code from one request to the next, and setting temperature to zero reduces that variation without removing it. 11 Two things follow. A skill cannot be the thing that enforces a rule, because nothing about loading it makes the agent comply. And a skill cannot be accepted the way a deterministic check is, on one green run, because the next run may differ. Without evals, a team cannot tell whether a skill helps, does nothing, or quietly makes the agent worse, and it cannot tell whether a model upgrade has changed any of that. 2 How it works Route the rule first. Every rule in the rule registry carries a route: gate, judgment or guidance. A skill serves the guidance route, and it may also help the agent meet a rule that a gate enforces. This site recommends a clear division of labour between validators and skills. When a validator can decide a rule, the validator carries it. A skill that touches the same rule teaches the agent why the rule exists and what a compliant change looks like, so the validator seldom has to fail. 6 7 A skill earns its place in work that turns on interpretation, where no deterministic check reaches. Write the skill for on-demand loading. Until the agent decides the skill applies, it sees only the name and description, so the description states plainly which tasks the skill is for. The main file carries what nearly every use of the skill needs. Material that only some uses need goes in separate files that the main file points to. Any step that must give an identical result every time is a script the agent executes, not prose it interprets. 3 7 The skill cites the identifiers of the rules it supports, so the registry can list every skill that touches a rule. That link is this site's recommended practice; no public source describes it. Build the eval set before trusting the skill. An eval gives the agent an input, lets it work, and applies grading logic to the result. Each case pairs a realistic request with a description of success and one or more graders, and a set tests both the cases where a behaviour should occur and the cases where it should not. 2 1 Skill evals also check activation: some cases name the skill, others are ordinary requests that never mention it, to see whether the agent picks it up unprompted. 10 Practitioner guidance suggests that a small set of tasks drawn from real failures is enough to start. 2 The expected behaviour comes from the specification and the rule, not from the skill's own text, so that the eval has an independent basis . For the customer-record export , an access-rule skill supports R-042: it guides the agent to return only the records the caller may read, and to stop and ask when the specification leaves the access rule open. Its eval set might hold these cases. Case Input Passes when Access rule left open A specification for the export that does not say who may read which records The agent stops and asks instead of choosing a rule Unprompted activation A plain request to speed up the export, with no mention of access The agent still loads the skill and keeps the filter Already correct An export whose access rule is settled and implemented The agent leaves the filtering as it is Excluded field A request to add a field the specification leaves out of the export The agent points out the conflict with the specification Review skill A change whose background worker runs a broader query than the request path The review skill reports the broader query against R-042 The skill does not enforce R-042; its validator is what fails a change that returns records the caller may not read. The skill makes that failure less likely, and the evals show by how much. Run each case more than once. Because output varies between runs, each case runs as several trials. 2 Two summaries matter. pass@k is the chance that at least one of k trials succeeds; pass^k, proposed in agent-benchmark research, is the chance that all k succeed, and it falls as k rises, which makes it the stricter measure of reliability. 12 2 A case that passes on some runs and fails on others is flaky and needs investigating, not re-running until it passes. 1 Choose the grader to fit the check. Code-based graders are fast, cheap and reproducible but brittle to valid variation; model-based graders handle nuance but are themselves non-deterministic and need calibrating against people; human graders are the most trustworthy and the slowest. Mechanical checks, such as whether the query filters by caller, belong in code. 2 1 A model used as a grader is the practice Zheng and colleagues studied as LLM-as-a-judge . In their study the strongest judge agreed with human preferences more than 80% of the time, about as often as people agree with each other, and it showed position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases. 13 Agreement with human grading is checked at the start and again from time to time. 2 9 Keep an evaluation history. Each run of the set compares the skill against a baseline: the same prompts without the skill, or the previous version of the skill. 1 Guidance on testing skills treats the aim as a score that can be compared over time. 10 This site recommends that the history record, for each skill version, the version of the eval set, the model and tool versions, the number of trials and the results, and that a skill ships only with such a history. That bar is recommended practice, not a published finding. Re-run when anything that shapes behaviour changes. Practitioner guidance runs evals on each change to the agent and on each model upgrade, and vendor guidance advises testing a skill with every model it will be used with. 2 7 After a change to the skill, every case runs again, not only the one that prompted the change. 1 This site adds two triggers as recommended practice: a change to a tool the skill relies on, and a change to any rule the skill cites, which also means revising the skill before its evals run. Once a skill is reliable, its cases become a regression suite that is expected to pass almost every time. 2 Keep the review skill advisory. A review skill reads a diff against the rules and reports findings tagged to rule identifiers. Böckeler's worked examples show inferential sensors addressing concerns such as semantic duplication only partially, where computational sensors catch duplicate code and coverage gaps reliably. 6 So the review skill proposes and a validator or a named person decides. It is evaluated like any other skill, with cases where it should raise a finding and cases where it should stay quiet. Until those results show how often it is right and how often it raises a false alarm, its findings inform reviewers and nothing more; what weight they carry after that is set in the assurance band of the map. Every finding costs a human reviewer some attention, so a noisy review skill is expensive. These are recommended practice. Decide when a practice becomes a skill. The usual trigger is repetition: the team finds itself typing the same guidance into agent sessions again and again. 7 Vendor guidance also suggests writing the evaluation cases first, from failures already seen, and the skill text after them. 3 7 Guidance that turns out to be a checkable rule goes to a validator, as described under routing above. This site recommends that someone answers for each skill: that person keeps its eval set current and removes the skill once nothing depends on it. Where it sits on the map Skills with evals is one of the five parts of the Engineering Kit , in the core band, the band that does the work. The kit is the versioned, installable package that carries a team's reusable harness. Next to skills sit the rule registry, which gives each skill the rules it supports; the validators, which enforce what a skill only encourages; the evidence schema , which fixes the shape of what a run records; and the adapters that bind the kit to the team's tools. In the map's core row, Harness engineering comes before the kit and supplies the split between guides and sensors; Workflows come after it and use skills inside their agent tasks and the review skill inside their checks. The feedback path feeds all of this: a procedure the agent keeps needing becomes a skill, and a failure in production becomes a new eval case. 5 Pitfalls A skill carrying a rule that must always hold. The only defence for the access rule is a paragraph in a skill. Sign: a rule routed to a gate in the registry has skills citing it but no validator. Shipping on one good run. The skill passed once, on one model, and nobody kept the result. Sign: no baseline comparison, a single trial per case, and no model version in the record. Evals that grade the skill against itself. Expected behaviour is copied from the skill's text, so the eval can only confirm what the skill already says. Sign: case descriptions that paraphrase the skill rather than the specification or the rule. Only happy-path cases. Every case expects the skill to produce a change. Sign: no case in which the skill should stay out of the way, and the skill starts rewriting exports that were already correct. An unchecked model grader. The model-based grader's scores are accepted without anyone reading transcripts. 2 Sign: no record of how often the grader and a person agree. Stale history. The model or a cited rule changed and the evals did not run again. Sign: the last recorded run names an older model, tool or rule version than the one in use. Re-running a flaky case until it passes. Sign: the same case alternates between pass and fail across runs, and the recorded result is only the last one. 1 Skills without a failure behind them. Skills written on speculation pile up, each one more thing to maintain. Sign: nobody can name the repeated miss a skill fixes, who answers for it, or when its evals last ran. Outside skills installed unread. A skill from another team or a public collection is someone else's instructions and code, acting with the agent's access. Sign: a skill in use that nobody on the team has read, or whose scripts nobody has checked for what they send or fetch. Putting it through the team's usual supply-chain review is recommended practice. Treating review findings as verdicts. The review skill's output decides merges, or reviewers dismiss it wholesale. Sign: merges approved or held on a finding alone, or findings closed without a reason. Related Validators : the deterministic checks that enforce what a skill only encourages. Rule registry : where each rule's identifier, route and owner live, and which skills cite it. Engineering Kit : the package that carries skills, evals and the other parts. Harness engineering : the discipline, including guides, sensors and the two kinds of control. Evidence schema : the fixed shape of what a run records. Workflows : where skills and the review skill are used in delivery. Terminology and the workflow catalog . Published with the Greek letter tau as its first character; spelled out here. ↩ ↩ Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena — Lianmin Zheng, Wei-Lin Chiang, Ying Sheng, et al., NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks Track — 2023-06 · source Examines using strong LLMs as judges of other models' answers; reports position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases and limited reasoning ability, and that the strongest judge reaches over 80% agreement with human preferences, the same level as agreement between humans. ↩ ↩ AI SDLC The software development lifecycle (SDLC) with AI agents doing part of the work in every phase, from intent and specification through design, build, verification, release and operation, while deterministic checks and human decisions stay where they are needed. Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. It cannot change the evidence schema, redefine a result state or waive a rule the core marks as never open to exception. coined Golden path The opinionated, supported way to build a kind of system that a platform offers its users, with templates and documentation, so that each team does not assemble its own tooling. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. On this site, an architecture rule expressed as a fitness function that runs with the build is a validator, and an architecture gate once it blocks. adopted ford-evolutionary-architectures Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a verify command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a few validators for rules the team has broken before, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency rules, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. It proposes; it cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Flexible and scalable, but itself non-deterministic and subject to position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so its grades are checked against human judgement before they are relied on. In an eval set it is one kind of grader, alongside code-based checks and human review. adopted zheng-llm-judge Evidence record What a run records in one fixed shape, as a by-product of the run rather than a report written afterwards: schema version, change and configuration revisions, kit version, the checks expected before the run, each check's result with its rule ID, status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending and taken, and an overall status derived from the rest. Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable), it timed out again after one retry, or the tool itself crashed. It is never reported as passed or skipped; what it means for a merge or release is decided in assurance. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. The name is this site's; the distinction is established, for example in SARIF's record of whether a tool's execution succeeded, and in test frameworks that report errors apart from failures. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives), a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended), a work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. It translates; it holds no rules, validator logic or schema. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. Adapted from Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters pattern (see that entry): his adapters sit at an application's ports, and this site applies the idea to the one layer of a kit that talks to outside tools. adapted cockburn-hexagonal Ports and adapters Alistair Cockburn's architecture pattern, also called hexagonal architecture: an application talks to the outside world only through ports, and a technology-specific adapter at each port translates between the outside device and the application, so the application can be driven by people, programs or tests and developed apart from the devices and databases it runs against. The Engineering Kit's tool adapters apply the same idea to the tools a kit runs against. adopted cockburn-hexagonal Anticorruption layer Eric Evans's domain-driven design pattern: an isolating layer that talks to another system through its existing interface and translates between the two models, so the other system's concepts do not reshape the model that uses it. A kit's adapters play this part between the kit's core and a tool's own vocabulary. adopted evans-ddd-reference Contract test Martin Fowler's name for a test that checks a test double still behaves like the real outside service it stands in for. It runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes. On this site, the contract suite a kit's core defines for each kind of adapter is the same idea pointed at the kit's own interface. adopted fowler-contract-test Consumer-driven contract Ian Robinson's service-evolution pattern: the consumers of a service state their expectations as tests, and the provider is checked against all of them, so it can change without breaking any consumer. adopted robinson-cdc Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. The idea of scaling test effort to risk comes from risk-based testing. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating state that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. Coined in this sense. Earlier uses of the phrase mean something else: Cusumano (1991) for Japanese firms that applied production-management discipline to large-scale software development, and Greenfield and Short (2004) for model-driven production of variants of a standard product. Recent writing on the "dark software factory", where agents produce software that no person reviews, is not what is meant either, nor is the industrial sense of identical outputs from a fixed process. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, plan and tasks, with clarification added where the specification leaves questions open. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. coined Independent basis for verification If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. The law does not say fewer controls are better. This site's recommendation follows from shrinking what is governed: narrow what the agent may produce first, on a few well-defined execution surfaces, then start with a small set of controls fitted to failures actually seen. adopted ashby
software-factory.html: Software factory The operating state that appears when delivery workflows share one set of rules, one evidence format and one feedback path, so that what production teaches changes what the next specification asks. Definition A software factory , in the sense this site uses, is the operating state that appears when enough delivery workflows share one set of rules, one format for evidence and one path for feedback, so that what production teaches changes what the next specification asks. It is not a product, a platform or a team that can be bought or set up on a given day. It is a property of how workflows that already run are connected. In an AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), the factory keeps people at every decision point: what makes it a factory is the shared thread of rule identifiers, evidence and recorded decisions, not unattended output. The sense is coined by this site, and the phrase has older meanings that are not intended here. Cusumano used it for Japanese firms that applied engineering and production-management discipline to large-scale software development 5 . Greenfield and Short used it for a configuration of languages, patterns, frameworks and tools that produces variants of a standard product from models 11 . Both describe standardised, repeatable production. Recent practitioner writing uses "dark software factory" for the far end of agent-assisted development, named after a factory run by robots with the lights out 14 , and one publicly described team works to the principles that code is neither written nor reviewed by people, with validation against scenarios in place of code review 17 . This site means neither identical outputs nor removed human review. Why it matters A single workflow improves one delivery decision. Several workflows that share nothing improve several decisions separately, and each lesson stays where it was learned. An incident is fixed in code, and the next specification repeats the gap that let it through. Each workflow keeps its own copy of the rules, and the copies drift until two workflows enforce different versions of the same rule. Evidence written in one format cannot be read by the next workflow unless someone copies it across by hand. Research on AI adoption suggests why the connections matter more as agents do more of the work. DORA's 2025 research describes AI's main role as an amplifier that magnifies the strengths of high-performing organisations and the dysfunctions of struggling ones, and associates higher AI adoption with increases in both software delivery throughput and instability 7 . Its 2024 research associated higher adoption with lower delivery throughput and stability, and suggested larger batch sizes as a reason 6 . DORA also groups customer feedback with value-stream visibility, small batches and team experimentation as capabilities that help predict delivery and organisational performance 9 . None of this is a finding about software factories: no public study shows that connecting agent workflows through shared rules, evidence and feedback improves outcomes. What follows is recommended practice, built on that adjacent evidence. How it works It emerges from workflows that already run No team starts by building a factory. It starts with one workflow that runs on real changes, such as pull-request verification, and adds another once the first is trusted. Shared parts appear when a second workflow needs something the first already has: it reads the access rule from the registry instead of keeping its own copy, and it reads check results in the format the first workflow already writes. Nothing moves into the shared layer until a workflow in use has needed it. Guidance on internal platforms points the same way. The Thoughtworks Technology Radar observes that teams often aim for too much of a platform vision too fast, and recommends growing a platform in increments 16 from what Team Topologies calls the thinnest viable platform, the smallest set of APIs, documentation and tools that speeds up the teams using it 15 . DORA lists quality internal platforms among the capabilities that amplify the benefits of AI 8 , so the risk lies in building shared parts ahead of the workflows that show what they must hold, not in having them. Growing the shared layer only from workflows that already run is this site's recommended practice. Three things are shared Rules. One rule registry holds the rules that apply across changes, each with an identifier, a route (a gate that blocks, a named person's judgment, or guidance) and an owner, and every workflow reads that registry rather than a copy of it. Material about a single change, such as its specification, plan and evidence, stays in version control with that change's code and is reviewed alongside it. Keeping it out of the registry keeps the registry small enough for its owners to keep current. Evidence. Every workflow writes its results in the one shape the evidence schema fixes, and the next workflow reads that record instead of asking the same questions again. A check that produced no verdict is recorded as could_not_run with its cause, and each human decision carries a reason code from a fixed list rather than free text. Because the codes are shared, a later workflow can act on a decision without interpreting prose, and a team can count how often each reason recurs across all its workflows. Keeping one list of reason codes for every workflow is recommended practice. Feedback. One feedback path decides where each lesson goes, and the change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. Böckeler calls the same practice the steering loop, in which people improve the harness (the context, tools, permissions and checks around an agent) based on recurring failures 2 . She also proposes harness templates, bundles of guides and sensors for a common type of service, which carry one team's controls to the next service of the same kind 2 . The Engineering Kit is the artefact that carries the shared rules, the deterministic checks (what Böckeler's sensors writing treats as computational sensors 3 ) and the evidence schema from one workflow and one team to the next. Production feedback reaches specification An incident review asks where the gap first became possible, not only where it showed. If nobody asked the question that would have exposed it, the action lands in specification readiness ; if a rule existed but nothing checked it, the action becomes a check tied to that rule's identifier. The site reliability engineering workbook notes that postmortem action items with little or no ownership are less likely to be resolved 10 , so each action names one owner and the stage it changes. Because every workflow reads the same registry and writes the same record, one change upstream reaches every later change of that kind. A new check or a tighter threshold does not start as a gate. It runs report-only first, recording what it would have blocked, and becomes required once its failures prove to be real problems rather than noise, since a gate that raises false alarms teaches people to override it. Repeated exceptions travel the same path: when one rule collects the same exception change after change, the pattern goes back to the rule's owner as a question about the rule or its route, instead of being granted once more. Both are this site's recommended practice. The running example across workflows In the customer-record export , a hypothetical feature that lets users export customer records, the specification readiness workflow finds that the specification does not yet say which roles may export which records, the question the access rule R-042 turns on. The product owner answers it before planning, because it concerns what the feature is for; the security owner, who owns R-042, confirms that the answer stays within the rule. The pull-request verification workflow reads that readiness record and runs the R-042 validator and the 50k-row load scenario tied to the volume-limit rule R-017. On the first pull request the validator fails on the background worker's broader query, and the load scenario reports could_not_run because the load-test tool is missing from the runner image. The worker's query is narrowed, the runner image gains the tool, and the checks run again. The release readiness workflow reads the resulting evidence record instead of asking the same questions again. In production, a scheduled full export, within R-017's limit but far larger than the 50k-row scenario, times out. The incident review traces the miss to specification: nobody asked what the largest export would be, so the scenario was sized for ordinary requests. Three changes follow. A larger load scenario joins the checks tied to R-017, the agent's evaluation set gains a case for the long-running export, and the readiness workflow now asks every export-like specification for the largest export it expects. The next export-like feature meets that question before planning starts. The identifiers R-042 and R-017 run through every record in the story; that shared thread, not any tool, is the factory. People keep the decisions In each workflow the agent does the drafting: open questions on a specification, plans, code and first reviews. Deterministic checks settle whatever can be settled mechanically, and named people decide what needs context no workflow holds, such as which roles may export which records. The agent never fills a decision field in the evidence record. Morris describes the human role as working on the loop: people build and adjust the loop that produces the work, rather than inspecting every output or leaving the agents to it 13 . Autonomy widens in that direction. When the same human correction keeps recurring, it becomes a rule and a check, and the person's review narrows to what the checks cannot decide; the decision point stays, while the mechanical part of it moves to a gate. Widening autonomy only by turning repeated judgments into checks, never by dropping an approval, is this site's recommended practice. Where it sits on the map The software factory is the fourth box of the core band (band 3, "what does the work"). The row reads Harness engineering, then the Engineering Kit , then Workflows, then the software factory: it comes after the discipline, the artefact and the unit of work. The map labels it the operating state and draws it with a dashed border, because it emerges from the other three rather than being built beside them. It is distinct from the operating model box in the enablement band, which covers team cadence and decision rights. In the lifecycle band, the map places each workflow in its phase, draws the loop by which incident feedback changes what specification asks, and runs a traceability spine from requirement to incident, linked by rule identifiers. The enablement band holds the runtime and tools, the people and roles, and that operating model, all of which the factory depends on. The assurance band holds the evidence record on every run and the measurement that shows whether the connections help. The adoption path's final stage, "Factory emerges", is where a team tests whether it has reached this state; that stage sets the criteria. Pitfalls Skill erosion. Bainbridge argued that when automation does most of a task, people are left monitoring it, and manual skills they no longer practise deteriorate, which makes taking over harder 1 . A survey of knowledge workers found that higher confidence in generative AI went with less critical thinking, on self-reported data 12 . The factory relies on human judgment at every decision point, so as recommended practice the people who hold those decisions still do some of the work unaided. The sign is people who struggle to take over when the agent or its checks are unavailable. Unowned or over-concentrated connections. The rules, evidence format and feedback path between workflows belong to no single workflow. Conway observed that organisations design systems that copy their communication structures 4 , so without an owner the connections tend to split along team lines. As recommended practice, the shared rules have one accountable owner, recorded by name, and ownership is confirmed again whenever people or teams change, not only when something goes wrong. The signs are rule changes queued behind one person, the same exception granted repeatedly for one rule, or nobody able to say who approves a change to the shared rules. Reading the factory as unattended throughput. Treating human decision points as the bottleneck to remove turns the factory into the lights-out sense this site does not mean, and larger batches of generated work were DORA's suggested reason for lower stability as AI adoption rose 6 . The sign is a proposal to waive a check or drop an approval to keep up with agent output. Lessons that never close. Incident reviews write actions that never reach the stage that owns the gap. The sign is the same kind of miss recurring after it has been reviewed, or actions with no single owner 10 . Related Workflows : the unit of work the factory connects, with its trigger, checks, human decision, evidence and owner. Harness engineering : the discipline behind the controls the factory shares. Engineering Kit : the versioned package that carries the shared rules, checks and evidence schema between workflows and teams. Rule registry : the shared rules, each with an identifier, a route and an owner. Evidence schema : the fixed shape of the record every workflow writes and the next one reads. Validators , Skills with evals and Adapters : the kit's other parts. Workflow catalog : the list of workflows the factory draws on. Terminology : the glossary entry and the credit for each term. Sources Cusumano, Japan's Software Factories : an earlier, production-management sense of the term 5 . Greenfield and Short, Software Factories : the model-driven sense of the term 11 . Morris on people working on the loop 13 ; Böckeler on the steering loop, harness templates and sensors 2 3 . DORA's 2024 and 2025 research on AI adoption, its AI capabilities model and its customer feedback capability 6 7 8 9 .
