Cited as a recent use of the term in a different sense. ↩ ↩ AI SDLC The software development lifecycle (SDLC) with AI agents doing part of the work in every phase, from intent and specification through design, build, verification, release and operation, while deterministic checks and human decisions stay where they are needed. Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. It cannot change the evidence schema, redefine a result state or waive a rule the core marks as never open to exception. coined Golden path The opinionated, supported way to build a kind of system that a platform offers its users, with templates and documentation, so that each team does not assemble its own tooling. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. On this site, an architecture rule expressed as a fitness function that runs with the build is a validator, and an architecture gate once it blocks. adopted ford-evolutionary-architectures Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a verify command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a few validators for rules the team has broken before, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency rules, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. It proposes; it cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Flexible and scalable, but itself non-deterministic and subject to position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so its grades are checked against human judgement before they are relied on. In an eval set it is one kind of grader, alongside code-based checks and human review. adopted zheng-llm-judge Evidence record What a run records in one fixed shape, as a by-product of the run rather than a report written afterwards: schema version, change and configuration revisions, kit version, the checks expected before the run, each check's result with its rule ID, status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending and taken, and an overall status derived from the rest. Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable), it timed out again after one retry, or the tool itself crashed. It is never reported as passed or skipped; what it means for a merge or release is decided in assurance. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. The name is this site's; the distinction is established, for example in SARIF's record of whether a tool's execution succeeded, and in test frameworks that report errors apart from failures. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives), a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended), a work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. It translates; it holds no rules, validator logic or schema. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. Adapted from Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters pattern (see that entry): his adapters sit at an application's ports, and this site applies the idea to the one layer of a kit that talks to outside tools. adapted cockburn-hexagonal Ports and adapters Alistair Cockburn's architecture pattern, also called hexagonal architecture: an application talks to the outside world only through ports, and a technology-specific adapter at each port translates between the outside device and the application, so the application can be driven by people, programs or tests and developed apart from the devices and databases it runs against. The Engineering Kit's tool adapters apply the same idea to the tools a kit runs against. adopted cockburn-hexagonal Anticorruption layer Eric Evans's domain-driven design pattern: an isolating layer that talks to another system through its existing interface and translates between the two models, so the other system's concepts do not reshape the model that uses it. A kit's adapters play this part between the kit's core and a tool's own vocabulary. adopted evans-ddd-reference Contract test Martin Fowler's name for a test that checks a test double still behaves like the real outside service it stands in for. It runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes. On this site, the contract suite a kit's core defines for each kind of adapter is the same idea pointed at the kit's own interface. adopted fowler-contract-test Consumer-driven contract Ian Robinson's service-evolution pattern: the consumers of a service state their expectations as tests, and the provider is checked against all of them, so it can change without breaking any consumer. adopted robinson-cdc Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. The idea of scaling test effort to risk comes from risk-based testing. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating state that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. Coined in this sense. Earlier uses of the phrase mean something else: Cusumano (1991) for Japanese firms that applied production-management discipline to large-scale software development, and Greenfield and Short (2004) for model-driven production of variants of a standard product. Recent writing on the "dark software factory", where agents produce software that no person reviews, is not what is meant either, nor is the industrial sense of identical outputs from a fixed process. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, plan and tasks, with clarification added where the specification leaves questions open. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. coined Independent basis for verification If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. The law does not say fewer controls are better. This site's recommendation follows from shrinking what is governed: narrow what the agent may produce first, on a few well-defined execution surfaces, then start with a small set of controls fitted to failures actually seen. adopted ashby
validators.html: Validators A validator is a deterministic check, written as code and tied to rule identifiers, that runs the same way locally and in CI, reports passed, failed, skipped or could_not_run, and can block a merge once it has earned trust. Definition A validator is a deterministic check, written as code, that enforces one or more rules from a team's rule registry and names those rule identifiers in every result it reports. It behaves identically on a developer's machine, inside a coding agent's session and in continuous integration (CI). It returns one of four results: passed, failed, skipped or could_not_run . Once it has proved trustworthy, it can block a merge. The term is this site's adaptation of Birgitta Böckeler's computational sensor: a feedback control that is deterministic and fast, run by ordinary computation rather than by a model, in contrast to inferential controls such as AI code review. 1 2 A validator usually wraps an existing tool, such as a linter, a type checker, a test suite or a dependency-rule checker. What turns the tool into a validator is the contract around it: the rule it answers to, the result it reports, and the same behaviour wherever it runs. A validator differs from its neighbours in specific ways. A unit test checks that code does what its author intended, while a validator checks a rule the team has agreed on, and may use tests to do it. A linter is one possible engine inside a validator; on its own it has no rule identifier and no defined result for "could not run". A review skill , an agent that reads a diff against the rules and reports findings, is inferential: it proposes, and it cannot block. 2 Why it matters In an AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), the volume of change rises faster than the capacity to review it. A rule that lives only in a guidance document or in a reviewer's memory is applied unevenly, and the unevenness grows with the volume. Böckeler separates computational controls, which are deterministic and fast, from inferential ones, which are slower, more expensive and less deterministic. 1 Her worked examples treat computational sensors as cheap enough to run on every change, with inferential review kept for what deterministic tools cannot judge. 2 One model vendor's published account of harness engineering on a large codebase describes the same move: architectural constraints enforced through automated checks rather than through reminders. 14 Every rule a machine can check the same way each time is one less thing a person has to remember to look for. The contract around the check is what makes this safe. Without it, familiar failures follow. A check that behaves differently locally and in CI sends developers and agents after failures they cannot reproduce, whereas continuous-integration practice expects any developer to be able to run the mainline build on their own machine. 5 A check that reports a missing tool as "no findings" quietly removes a gate. A check that blocks before anyone trusts it gets bypassed or switched off. A flaky check teaches people to re-run until the result turns green. How it works One rule, one identifier Each validator declares the rule identifiers it enforces, and each finding it reports carries the identifier of the rule it concerns. In the customer-record export , rule R-042 says that every query path serving an export filters by the records the caller is allowed to read. The access validator for R-042 reports each finding against R-042, with the file and query that break it. SARIF, the OASIS standard format for static-analysis output, keys results the same way: each result carries a ruleId , the stable identifier of the rule that was evaluated to produce it. 17 The site recommends the link for three reasons. A finding leads straight to the rule's text and its owner. The registry can show which rules are enforced by a validator and which still depend on judgment. When a rule retires, the validators that enforce it are easy to find and retire with it. Not every rule suits a validator. The test is whether a program can detect a violation and give the same verdict every time it runs on the same input. Rules about how code is arranged and what it may depend on usually pass: forbidden imports between modules, committed credentials, disallowed licences, interface schemas that must not break. Rules about purpose usually do not, and they stay with named people. In the export example, R-042 passes the test, because a program can find a query path that reads customer records without the caller's filter; whether the exported fields are the ones users actually need does not. A rule that passes the test is routed to a gate in the Rule registry , and its validator is built next. The same run everywhere A validator has one entry point, pinned tool versions and one configuration. The developer's machine, the agent's session and the CI pipeline all call that entry point; CI calls the check and never redefines it. The Engineering Kit 's verify command runs a project's validators this way. The kit supplies the mechanism (the entry point, the four results and the report format), and the project supplies the meaning: which of its rules have validators, and what their limits are. Continuous-integration practice asks for a fast build that any developer can reproduce locally, and a validator inherits both expectations: fast enough to run on every change, and reproducible off the shared build. 5 Reporting the result Every run ends in exactly one of four results, each tagged with the rule identifier: passed : the rule was evaluated against the change and no violation was found. failed : a violation was found. The result gives the rule, the location and what is wrong, and links to the full report. skipped : the rule does not apply to this change, for example because the change touches no export path. The validator decides this from a declared condition, never by guessing. could_not_run : the rule applies and the check was required, but no verdict was produced, because a tool was missing, an environment was unavailable, the run timed out or the tool crashed. SARIF draws the same line between "did the tool run" and "what did it find". Each run records whether the tool's execution succeeded separately from its results, and the format has a result kind for a rule that was not evaluated because it does not apply. Its informative appendix warns that when the tool reports an execution error, its results cannot be assumed complete. 17 In SARIF's terms, passed corresponds to pass , failed to fail and skipped to notApplicable . Could_not_run is this site's own term; the nearest SARIF equivalent is an unsuccessful execution. A validator detects that it cannot run by checking its prerequisites before it evaluates anything: the tool is present at the expected version, the environment answers, and the test data exists. It reads the tool's actual output rather than trusting the exit code alone, since SARIF notes that not every program exits with 0 on success and non-zero on failure. 17 When the validator never starts at all, it cannot report anything, and SARIF expects the component that launched the tool to write the record instead. 17 In practice, the runner treats a required validator that produced no result as could_not_run. Could_not_run must never be reported as skipped. At least one change host counts a skipped required status check as satisfied, 9 so a missing environment reported as "skipped" lets the change through unchecked. In the export example, R-017, the volume-limit rule, states a row limit for a single export, and its check runs the 50k-row load scenario. On the first export pull request the load-test tool is missing from the runner image, so the check reports could_not_run and names the missing tool. It does not report failed, because the change is not at fault, and it does not report skipped, because the rule applies. The validator only reports. What each result means for a merge or release decision is set in the assurance band of the map, and the kit-wide definition of could_not_run is on the Engineering Kit page. From report-only to required A new validator first runs in report-only mode: it runs on every pull request and its findings are visible, but it cannot stop a merge. Policy engines ship modes for exactly this. One open-source cluster policy engine's dry-run mode lets new constraints be tested in a running cluster without enforcing them, and its warn mode also tells the requester why a request would have been denied. 7 A container orchestrator's built-in admission policies offer deny, warn and audit as separate actions. 12 CI platforms have a weaker counterpart: one platform's documentation describes a job allowed to fail, which shows a warning while the pipeline still counts as successful. 10 A finding that shows only as a warning on a passing job is easy to miss, so report-only results need a place where people actually read them. No public source says when a validator should start to block, so this is recommended practice. A validator enters report-only mode with an owner and a date by which the decision is due. The decision comes from its record, not the calendar. Where its failures pointed at real problems that people fixed in the code, it becomes a required check. Where they were mostly noise, the validator is corrected and the date moves, or the validator is retired. The switch to required is itself a reviewed change, so the evidence shows when the check began to block. In the export example, the access validator for R-042 is a required check that covers background workers as well as the request path. A background worker's broader query had been a recurring finding in human review, and that repeated finding is why the validator was extended to cover worker queries. On the first export pull request it reports failed, tagged R-042, and points to the worker's query, which reads more records than the caller may see. Timeouts Each validator sets its own time limit and does not rely on a runner's default, which may be far longer than the check needs. A timeout is never a pass. Check platforms keep "timed out" as a conclusion separate from success, 8 and one test runner's timeout plugin ends a hanging test by failing it or by stopping the process. 16 The site recommends one retry, to rule out a transient fault in the environment. If the retry also times out, the validator reports could_not_run, stating the limit and how far the run got. The exception is a rule that is itself a time budget, such as a response-time limit; there, running out of time is the violation, and the result is failed. Flaky checks A flaky check passes and fails on the same code, so a failure stops being a reliable signal: real failures get overlooked, and time goes on re-runs. 15 Martin Fowler argues that non-deterministic tests damage trust in the whole suite. He treats quarantine as a short-term measure that needs a limit on how many tests it holds or how long they stay there. 6 Google's testing team has described re-running failed tests and automatically quarantining the flakiest ones, with a bug filed for each. 11 One empirical study of fixes to flaky tests in open-source projects reports asynchronous waits, concurrency and test-order dependency as the most common causes. 13 How a workflow run treats a check that failed and then passed is on the Workflows page. Checks that depend on timing or shared environments, such as the 50k-row load scenario for R-017, are the most exposed, since asynchronous waits and concurrency are among the causes Luo and colleagues found most often. 13 Fitness functions for architecture rules Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons and Patrick Kua introduced the architectural fitness function in Building Evolutionary Architectures , borrowing the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. 4 18 Fitness function-driven development writes these checks first, in the manner of test-driven development, so that architectural conformance gets feedback during development rather than after it. 3 An architecture rule becomes a validator when it is expressed as a structural check that runs with the build, such as an architecture test in the application's own test suite or a dependency-rule checker's configuration. In the export example, such rules might say that the export feature reaches customer records only through the data-access layer, that the domain layer depends on nothing above it, and that no dependency cycles exist between modules. Böckeler's worked examples include dependency rules, written with the agent's help, that enforce a codebase's module layers. 2 The recommended practice is to begin with structural rules this codebase has already been seen to break, and to add them one at a time, so that each rule's failures are understood before the next rule arrives. A failure message that names the rule, the offending dependency and the permitted alternative lets a coding agent correct its own change without a person translating. Keeping the validator honest An agent asked to make a check pass may find it easier to change the check than the code. As recommended practice, a validator's code, configuration and limits sit outside what an agent may change unsupervised: a change that alters a validator and the code it checks at the same time goes to a person for review. Tests an agent writes to satisfy a validator are reviewed for what they actually establish, and a test that has never been seen to fail without the behaviour it checks is weak evidence. Ready to ship No public source sets a release bar for a check of this kind, so the following is this site's recommended practice. A validator is ready to ship in the kit, even in report-only mode, when: it gives the same result locally, in the agent's session and in CI; it has a known-bad example that must fail and a known-good example that must pass, both kept with the validator and run whenever it changes; it reports could_not_run for each prerequisite it depends on, and never reports passed or skipped when a prerequisite is missing; it has its own time limit and a named owner; each failure carries the rule identifier, the location, what is wrong and a link to the evidence. Where it sits on the map Validators sit in the core band, band 3 of the map ("what does the work"), as one of the five parts inside the Engineering Kit box. Before a validator comes its rule: a rule routed to a gate in the Rule registry becomes a validator here. Alongside are skills, which guide what an agent tries to do rather than checking the result, and so meet a different acceptance bar (see Skills with evals ). After the validator, each result lands in the evidence record , whose fields are fixed on the Evidence schema page. Adapters bind validators to a particular CI runner and change host without making them depend on either. In the vocabulary of Harness engineering , validators are the computational sensors, while skills and instructions are guides. 1 Every workflow calls validators at its checks step (see Workflows ). The assurance band of the map decides what their results mean for merge and release. Pitfalls Report-only with no end. Validators stay non-blocking long after their findings became actionable. Sign to watch: validators past their end date, and report-only findings that nobody acts on. Blocking before trust. A validator becomes required while it is still noisy. Sign to watch: requests to bypass it, or the check quietly switched off. A missing prerequisite reported as clean. A validator that could not run reports passed or skipped. Sign to watch: a required check that reports no findings on a run that scanned zero files or never reached its environment. Retry to green. Failures that pass on a second run are counted as passes. Sign to watch: rising re-run counts, and reports that show only the final pass of a check that failed first. Drift between local and CI. The pipeline runs its own version of the check. Sign to watch: "it passes on my machine" in pull-request threads, or a CI configuration that repeats the check's logic. Failures nobody can act on. A red status with no rule identifier, location or evidence link. Sign to watch: questions in the pull request about what failed and why. The check weakened by the change it checks. An agent relaxes a validator to get a pass. Sign to watch: a single change that edits both a validator or its limits and the code it checks. Orphaned validators. Checks keep running after their rule has changed or retired. Sign to watch: findings with no rule identifier, or identifiers the registry no longer holds. Evidence schema : the fields that record each validator's result. Skills with evals : the probabilistic counterpart to validators, and why its bar differs. Adapters : how validators bind to a CI runner and change host. Harness engineering : the discipline in which validators are the computational sensors. Workflows : where validators run as the checks step of each delivery decision. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. It cannot change the evidence schema, redefine a result state or waive a rule the core marks as never open to exception. coined Golden path The opinionated, supported way to build a kind of system that a platform offers its users, with templates and documentation, so that each team does not assemble its own tooling. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. On this site, an architecture rule expressed as a fitness function that runs with the build is a validator, and an architecture gate once it blocks. adopted ford-evolutionary-architectures Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a verify command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a few validators for rules the team has broken before, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency rules, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. It proposes; it cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Flexible and scalable, but itself non-deterministic and subject to position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so its grades are checked against human judgement before they are relied on. In an eval set it is one kind of grader, alongside code-based checks and human review. adopted zheng-llm-judge Evidence record What a run records in one fixed shape, as a by-product of the run rather than a report written afterwards: schema version, change and configuration revisions, kit version, the checks expected before the run, each check's result with its rule ID, status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending and taken, and an overall status derived from the rest. Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable), it timed out again after one retry, or the tool itself crashed. It is never reported as passed or skipped; what it means for a merge or release is decided in assurance. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. The name is this site's; the distinction is established, for example in SARIF's record of whether a tool's execution succeeded, and in test frameworks that report errors apart from failures. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives), a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended), a work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. It translates; it holds no rules, validator logic or schema. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. Adapted from Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters pattern (see that entry): his adapters sit at an application's ports, and this site applies the idea to the one layer of a kit that talks to outside tools. adapted cockburn-hexagonal Ports and adapters Alistair Cockburn's architecture pattern, also called hexagonal architecture: an application talks to the outside world only through ports, and a technology-specific adapter at each port translates between the outside device and the application, so the application can be driven by people, programs or tests and developed apart from the devices and databases it runs against. The Engineering Kit's tool adapters apply the same idea to the tools a kit runs against. adopted cockburn-hexagonal Anticorruption layer Eric Evans's domain-driven design pattern: an isolating layer that talks to another system through its existing interface and translates between the two models, so the other system's concepts do not reshape the model that uses it. A kit's adapters play this part between the kit's core and a tool's own vocabulary. adopted evans-ddd-reference Contract test Martin Fowler's name for a test that checks a test double still behaves like the real outside service it stands in for. It runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes. On this site, the contract suite a kit's core defines for each kind of adapter is the same idea pointed at the kit's own interface. adopted fowler-contract-test Consumer-driven contract Ian Robinson's service-evolution pattern: the consumers of a service state their expectations as tests, and the provider is checked against all of them, so it can change without breaking any consumer. adopted robinson-cdc Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. The idea of scaling test effort to risk comes from risk-based testing. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating state that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. Coined in this sense. Earlier uses of the phrase mean something else: Cusumano (1991) for Japanese firms that applied production-management discipline to large-scale software development, and Greenfield and Short (2004) for model-driven production of variants of a standard product. Recent writing on the "dark software factory", where agents produce software that no person reviews, is not what is meant either, nor is the industrial sense of identical outputs from a fixed process. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, plan and tasks, with clarification added where the specification leaves questions open. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. coined Independent basis for verification If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. The law does not say fewer controls are better. This site's recommendation follows from shrinking what is governed: narrow what the agent may produce first, on a few well-defined execution surfaces, then start with a small set of controls fitted to failures actually seen. adopted ashby

Item enters the backlog Draft classification (feature, bug, spike, production bug); propose change categories, size and initial risk tier from the description Required intake fields present; size within the feature cap; categories from the allowed set Product owner classifies; tech lead confirms lane Intake record All First Backlog grooming; project initiation; rough-order-of-magnitude estimate; scope and MVP definition PM / BA; sponsor Backlog item; ROM estimate; project management plan Absorbs change-risk classification. Sizing rule lives here. W02 0 Security discovery and baseline Which security objectives, regulations and baseline requirements apply to this product or feature set? New product, or a feature that introduces a new data class, integration or tenant boundary Draft gap analysis of the proposed scope against the security baseline; list applicable regulations and certifications Baseline checklist completeness; every baseline item has a status Security owner confirms objectives and gaps to close Baseline and gap record All Later SDL discovery; security baselines and gap analysis; required certifications Sponsor; security Security objectives; gap analysis Runs rarely. Could fold into W04 for small products. W03 1 Design-to-specification handoff Is the design source stable and complete enough to specify from? Wireframes or prototype marked done Derive a UI capability description from the design source: screens, flows, states, responsive behavior Design asset versioned and locked (gold master); all interactive states enumerated; only design-system tokens referenced Design owner signs off the baseline Handoff record UI First User research and personas; wireframes to hi-fi mockups; usability review and sign-off; asset handoff UX / Design Wireframes; mockups; prototype; design-system components Gold-master governance lives here. W04 1 Specification readiness Is the specification ready to plan from? Specification marked ready for planning Scan for ambiguity, missing edge cases, untestable acceptance criteria, unstated non-functional requirements; propose risk tier and open questions Required sections present; every acceptance criterion has an identifier; mandatory questions have recorded answers Product owner resolves intent; engineering or security owner confirms constraints Readiness record All First Requirement gathering and review; SRS; use cases and user stories; success criteria and KPIs; clarifications; requirement sign-off PM / BA SRS; use cases; acceptance criteria; sign-off The workflow that configures the rest. W05 1 Brownfield pre-flight analysis What does the existing system already do here, and what must not change? Specification touches existing code (not greenfield) Map affected components, current behavior, conventions, implicit rules and dependencies from the codebase Symbol and dependency navigation is deterministic (language server or equivalent); report cites file locations Architect confirms or corrects the analysis Analysis report attached to the specification All First Feasibility and constraints; impact analysis; technical spike input Architecture; senior developer Often nothing written Traditional counterpart was usually informal. W06 1 Threat modeling Which threats apply to this change, and which mitigations are required? Specification touches authentication, authorization, data classes, external integrations or trust boundaries Draft threat model from the specification and architecture; propose mitigations mapped to acceptance criteria Every trust boundary named in the plan has an entry; every mitigation traces to a criterion or a rule Security owner validates the model and required mitigations Threat model record API Data Later Threat modeling (preparation, analysis, mitigations, validation); threat model updates Senior engineers; project managers; security Threat model SDL activity. Also updated at plan time. W07 1 Spike Which option, or is this feasible at all? A bounded question with a time box Explore options; prototype; summarize trade-offs with evidence Time box enforced; output in the required decision-record format Decision recorded with rationale; does not count as delivery throughput Decision record All Later Technical spike; proof of concept; feasibility study; high-level solution options Architecture; development Demo; verbal conclusion Low frequency; keep in catalog, low priority. W08 2 Plan and architecture conformance Is the technical approach acceptable, and which gates apply? Readiness record accepted Draft plan from the specification; check against the constitution; identify boundaries crossed and change categories; draft gate declaration Constitution rules routed to gates are checked; gate declaration committed with lane, categories and named reviewers Tech lead owns the plan; architect approves exceptions Plan with gate declaration All First System and data design; system design document; architecture diagram; design review and standards; component and module design Architecture; development SDD; architecture diagram; DFD; tech-design notes Where the risk tier becomes the gate set. W09 2 API contract design Is the interface contract agreed before implementation starts? Plan declares a new or changed API surface Draft or update the contract from the specification; flag breaking changes and undocumented surface Schema valid; breaking-change diff against the current version; versioning rule applied API owner approves; consumers notified for breaking changes Contract record API First Interface and API contracts; interface design for user and other systems Architecture API specification (OpenAPI or equivalent) Contract-first principle. W10 2 Data model and migration plan Is the data change designed safely, with a way back? Plan declares a data model change or migration Draft schema change, migration sequence and rollback; identify affected data and consumers Schema diff; migration and rollback scripts present; data classification recorded Data owner approves the design Data design record Data First Database design; ER diagram; tables, relationships, keys and constraints Architecture; DBA ER diagram; data design Execution is W16. W11 2 Security design review Does the design meet the security requirements and mitigations? Plan for a change with tier-3 security categories Review the plan against the baseline and threat model; list unmitigated threats Every required mitigation traces to a task or a rule Security reviewer (tier 3) approves Security design record API Data Later Security design review; security requirements; privacy impact assessment Development team; security expert Review record SDL activity. Could be a gate inside W08 for lower tiers. W12 2 Task traceability and test planning Is the work ready to start (definition of ready)? Plan accepted Generate tasks from the plan; map every acceptance criterion to implementation and test tasks; classify each criterion under the testing contract No orphan criteria; no task without a criterion; test tasks precede implementation tasks; stable task identifiers Dev lead confirms sequencing; QA lead owns the testing-contract classification Tasks file with traceability All First Task breakdown; sprint planning; effort estimation; test plan and strategy; testability review; traceability to requirements Development; QA Tickets; estimates; test plan; traceability matrix Absorbs STLC test planning. W13 3 Task execution loop Is this task done to the agreed standard? Task picked up Implement the task; run the kit's verify command; self-correct within the retry limit; write the commit message with task identifier Lint, type check, unit tests, sandbox and permission boundaries, command restrictions, branch protection Developer directs and inspects; stops the loop on repeated failure Commit linked to the task with check results All Floor Feature implementation; unit testing; coding standards; branch and merge; integration builds Development Commits; unit tests The verify command is the floor. No agent needed to start. W14 3 Documentation generation Is the documentation current with the change? Change touches a public surface, a runbook or an architecture decision Generate or update API docs from the contract, ADR drafts, runbook steps and user-facing notes Docs diff present when a public surface changed; links resolve; generated sections marked Owner reviews substance, not formatting Docs record All Later Tech-design notes; code documentation; user documentation; training material (docs only) Development; PM Wiki pages; comments; manuals AGN: docs generated inline rather than afterwards. W15 3 Dependency change May this library or version enter the codebase? Manifest or lockfile changes Summarize what the dependency is for and what it replaces; note maintenance signals License policy; vulnerability scan; version pinning; approved-source check Architect approves new dependencies; security owner for flagged ones Dependency record All Floor Third-party software tracking and inventory; library approval; open-source licensing review Senior technical lead; security Inventory; wiki entry Scanning is a floor check; approval is the workflow. W16 3 Data change execution Is this migration safe to run, and can it be undone? Migration script committed Draft migration and rollback; identify affected records and downtime window Migration rehearsal on representative data; rollback rehearsal; row-count and integrity checks Data owner approves the run Rehearsal and rollback record Data First Migration script review; DBA review; legacy data migration DBA; development Reviewed script; backup plan Pairs with W10. W17 4 Acceptance-test generation and execution Does the change meet its acceptance criteria? Implementation tasks complete, or on every pull request for the criteria in scope Generate test scenarios from acceptance criteria; separate generated from pre-existing tests; propose test data Tests execute in CI; results stored with criterion identifiers; changed-code coverage against baseline QA lead judges scenario adequacy and coverage gaps Test results with criterion identifiers All First Test-case design; test-data setup; test execution; defect logging; regression testing; functional and integration testing QA Test cases; execution log; defect tickets; test summary Absorbs four STLC stages. W18 4 Security verification Are the access and exposure boundaries intact for this change? Change carries a security category, or on every pull request for the floor checks Trace access paths through the change; explain threats introduced; propose remediation Access tests by identity; secret scanning; static analysis; dependency audit; dynamic analysis where an environment exists Security owner for tier-3 categories; otherwise the reviewer Security check record All Floor Static analysis; dynamic analysis; vulnerability scanning; fuzzing; security review; secure coding checklist Developers; QA; security expert Scan reports; review ticket Secret scanning and SAST are floor; access tests are first. W19 4 Performance verification Does the change stay within its performance budget? Change carries a performance category, or touches a budgeted path Select scenarios relevant to the change; analyze regressions against baseline Budget thresholds; regression against baseline; scenario executed in a representative environment Owner accepts or rejects a budget change Performance record All Later Non-functional review; performance and load testing Architecture; QA Load test report Needs a load environment; often could-not-run at first. W20 4 Accessibility and visual regression Is the interface still correct, accessible and consistent? Change touches interface files Identify changed screens and states; draft what a person should look at Accessibility rules; visual diff; both themes; all component states; design-system tokens only Design owner judges intent and acceptable differences Interface check record UI First Design QA versus build; pixel and interaction review; accessibility checks; visual-regression review; usability testing UX / Design; QA Screenshots; a11y report FRP UI variant. W21 4 API contract conformance Does the implementation match the agreed contract? Change touches an endpoint Diff contract and implementation; flag undocumented surface used by clients Contract tests; schema validation; breaking-change detection; consumer contracts where they exist API owner approves version bumps Conformance record API First Interface testing; integration testing between modules; consumer verification Development; QA Integration test results FRP API variant. W22 4 System integration and acceptance evidence Does the integrated system behave, and does the business accept it? Feature validated at pull-request level; SIT entry criteria met Assemble the evidence pack; draft UAT scripts from acceptance criteria; summarize open defects and dispositions SIT entry evidence present; environment and configuration version recorded; every criterion has a disposition QA lead runs SIT, including manual paths that span hardware, firmware and cloud; business owner signs acceptance SIT and acceptance record All Later System testing; user acceptance testing; UAT coordination; business sign-off; test summary; acceptance contract QA; PM; business Test summary; UAT sign-off; acceptance contract Human-led; the agent assembles evidence. Manual SIT stays where paths cannot be reproduced in CI. W23 5 Pull-request verification Is this change ready to merge? Pull request marked ready; revision changes Compare the diff with the specification; trace affected paths; draft findings with locations and reasons; summarize All required checks for the tier; expected checks recorded before results; enforcement status verified Reviewer decides on design, unresolved questions and adequacy of verification Verification record All First Code review; design-adherence review; peer review Development; architecture Approval comment Aggregates W17-W21 results. W24 5 Design and architecture review Is the design acceptable given its trade-offs? Tier-3 change, or an explicit architecture decision Summarize the decision, alternatives considered and consequences None that can be mechanized Named specialist reviewer with capacity Design decision record (ADR) All Later Architecture board; design review; standards governance Architecture Meeting minutes; ADR Judgment-only workflow; the agent only prepares. W25 6 Release readiness Is this release safe to deploy? Release candidate tagged Aggregate evidence across the changes; draft release notes and known risks; check for missing records All required records present and current for the candidate revision; rollback path demonstrated; configuration version recorded; final license and security gap checks Release owner approves; mandatory organizational controls (CAB, security sign-off) unchanged Release record All First Go/no-go input; release-readiness review; release notes; stakeholder comms; final security gap analysis; final privacy review; open-source licensing review; test closure PM; DevOps; QA; security Release notes; approval; acceptance contract Absorbs STLC test closure and SDL release activities. W26 6 Deployment and post-deploy verification Is the deployment healthy, or do we roll back? Deployment started Compare observed health to expected; summarize anomalies Health checks; smoke tests; toggles; deployment event and environment recorded; rollback rehearsed On-call decides rollback or proceed; hypercare owner named Deployment record All First Deployment plan and checklist; production environment setup; smoke and sanity; rollback plan; config and secrets; deployment notice; deployment strategy (phased, rolling, pilot) DevOps / Platform Deployment notice; runbook Deployment strategy is a plan input, not a workflow. W27 7 Incident remediation Mitigate now, roll back, or fix forward? Alert or incident opened Triage; correlate logs, metrics and recent changes; propose remediation; draft the fix as a pull request Rollback available; proposed fix passes pull-request verification before deploy On-call decides the response Incident record All Later Incident response; incident verification; defect resolution; hotfix readiness; corrective maintenance DevOps / SRE; development; QA Incident ticket; hotfix AGN: agent-assisted remediation. Never auto-deploys. W28 7 Incident-to-development feedback What must change upstream so this does not recur? Incident closed, or escaped defect classified Propose root cause; identify which check passed wrongly, was absent, or was bypassed; draft the regression case Proposed test reproduces the failure before the fix and passes after Owner picks the conversion (criterion, test, validator, eval) and the workflow it lands in Feedback record linked to the upstream change All First Post-mortem; root-cause analysis; defect-driven backlog; tech-debt and improvement backlog; feedback loop Development; QA; PM RCA document; backlog items The loop that makes the software factory real. W29 7 Vulnerability response Are we exposed, and is the patch verified? Advisory published, or scanner finding Map the advisory to affected components and versions; draft the patch change Dependency audit; patch verification tests; exposure window recorded Security owner sets urgency and accepts closure Response record All First Third-party software tracking and review; external vulnerability disclosure and response; security updates Senior technical lead; security Spreadsheet; tickets Scanning floor exists via W15. W30 7 Usage and feedback intake What should change based on how the product is actually used? Review cadence, or a threshold in analytics or support volume Summarize analytics, support tickets and UX feedback into candidate backlog items with evidence links None deterministic; every candidate cites its source Product owner prioritizes; enters W01 Feedback digest All Later Adoption tracking; UX analytics; feedback-driven design backlog; benefits realization; perfective maintenance PM; UX / Design Analytics dashboards; backlog Feeds W01. Low deterministic content. W31 7 Decommission and data disposal Can this component or data be retired safely and compliantly? Retirement decision, or retention period expiry Inventory data, dependencies and consumers; list retention obligations Retention policy rules; dependency check for remaining consumers; key destruction verified Data owner and compliance approve Disposal record All Later Disposal; data retention and disposal; crypto-shredding Compliance; platform Disposal record SDL Disposal phase. Rare but regulated. W32 X Change control Is this change approved to proceed against the baseline? Any change that alters scope, a controlled artefact or a production system under change management Draft the change request with impact drawn from existing evidence records Change log entry present; linked evidence current; scope-change document attached when scope moved Designated approver or CAB, per the operating model Change record All First Change requests; scope-change documentation; change impact and approval; change log; audit trail; regression on changes PM / BA; architecture; DevOps Change request; change log Evidence links now; automation later. W33 X Exception handling May this requirement be departed from, for how long, and under what compensating control? A required check fails, or a control cannot be met Draft the exception with scope, rationale and compensating control Expiry enforced; underlying failed or missing check remains visible in evidence Designated gate owner approves; enterprise controls never waived here Exception record All First Waiver; risk acceptance Manager; security Email; risk register entry Operating-model rule; kit enforces visibility. W34 X Kit upgrade Adopt this kit version in this project? New kit release None required; optional summary of behavior changes init, doctor, verify; new validators report-only before they become required; enforcement verified Project owner accepts the upgrade Upgrade record All First Tooling or framework upgrade (ad hoc) Development; DevOps None No traditional counterpart worth mapping. W35 X Evaluation rerun Is this skill or model still acceptable after a change? Skill, prompt, adapter or model version changes The subject under test Evaluation suite against golden scenarios; report by scenario, not by count Owner reads which scenario failed and decides Evaluation report All Later None None None Exists only because agents do.
