backend / API; data / storage Applies-to column Variant paths Each variant selects a subset of workflows glossary.html#workflow What a workflow is AI SDLC The software development lifecycle (SDLC) with AI agents doing part of the work in every phase, from intent and specification through design, build, verification, release and operation, while deterministic checks and human decisions stay where they are needed. Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. It cannot change the evidence schema, redefine a result state or waive a rule the core marks as never open to exception. coined Golden path The opinionated, supported way to build a kind of system that a platform offers its users, with templates and documentation, so that each team does not assemble its own tooling. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. On this site, an architecture rule expressed as a fitness function that runs with the build is a validator, and an architecture gate once it blocks. adopted ford-evolutionary-architectures Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a verify command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a few validators for rules the team has broken before, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency rules, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. It proposes; it cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Flexible and scalable, but itself non-deterministic and subject to position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so its grades are checked against human judgement before they are relied on. In an eval set it is one kind of grader, alongside code-based checks and human review. adopted zheng-llm-judge Evidence record What a run records in one fixed shape, as a by-product of the run rather than a report written afterwards: schema version, change and configuration revisions, kit version, the checks expected before the run, each check's result with its rule ID, status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending and taken, and an overall status derived from the rest. Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable), it timed out again after one retry, or the tool itself crashed. It is never reported as passed or skipped; what it means for a merge or release is decided in assurance. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. The name is this site's; the distinction is established, for example in SARIF's record of whether a tool's execution succeeded, and in test frameworks that report errors apart from failures. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives), a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended), a work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. It translates; it holds no rules, validator logic or schema. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. Adapted from Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters pattern (see that entry): his adapters sit at an application's ports, and this site applies the idea to the one layer of a kit that talks to outside tools. adapted cockburn-hexagonal Ports and adapters Alistair Cockburn's architecture pattern, also called hexagonal architecture: an application talks to the outside world only through ports, and a technology-specific adapter at each port translates between the outside device and the application, so the application can be driven by people, programs or tests and developed apart from the devices and databases it runs against. The Engineering Kit's tool adapters apply the same idea to the tools a kit runs against. adopted cockburn-hexagonal Anticorruption layer Eric Evans's domain-driven design pattern: an isolating layer that talks to another system through its existing interface and translates between the two models, so the other system's concepts do not reshape the model that uses it. A kit's adapters play this part between the kit's core and a tool's own vocabulary. adopted evans-ddd-reference Contract test Martin Fowler's name for a test that checks a test double still behaves like the real outside service it stands in for. It runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes. On this site, the contract suite a kit's core defines for each kind of adapter is the same idea pointed at the kit's own interface. adopted fowler-contract-test Consumer-driven contract Ian Robinson's service-evolution pattern: the consumers of a service state their expectations as tests, and the provider is checked against all of them, so it can change without breaking any consumer. adopted robinson-cdc Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. The idea of scaling test effort to risk comes from risk-based testing. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating state that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. Coined in this sense. Earlier uses of the phrase mean something else: Cusumano (1991) for Japanese firms that applied production-management discipline to large-scale software development, and Greenfield and Short (2004) for model-driven production of variants of a standard product. Recent writing on the "dark software factory", where agents produce software that no person reviews, is not what is meant either, nor is the industrial sense of identical outputs from a fixed process. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, plan and tasks, with clarification added where the specification leaves questions open. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. coined Independent basis for verification If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. The law does not say fewer controls are better. This site's recommendation follows from shrinking what is governed: narrow what the agent may produce first, on a few well-defined execution surfaces, then start with a small set of controls fitted to failures actually seen. adopted ashby
workflows.html: Workflows A workflow is one delivery decision run end to end, with a trigger, an agent task, automated checks, a named human decision, an evidence record and one owner. Definition In the AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), a workflow is one delivery decision carried from the event that starts it to a recorded outcome. Its definition names nine parts: the trigger, the inputs it reads, the task the coding agent performs, the automated checks that run, the guardrails that bound the agent, the person who decides, the evidence it leaves, the place its lessons go, and one accountable owner. "Is this change ready to merge?" is a workflow . So is "Is this specification ready for planning?" The word is used here in this narrow sense, which this site coined; the parts list is the site's recommended definition, not an industry standard. The idea has a long lineage. Lean value-stream mapping diagrams every step in the material and information flows needed to deliver a product or service 15 , and lean practice gives the whole stream an accountable manager who may not own the people and resources in it 14 . DORA recommends value stream mapping to see how work flows from idea to production and where it stalls 7 . A workflow is a smaller unit than a value stream: the single step in which a decision is made, defined tightly enough that an agent can take part in it without taking the decision. A workflow is not the same as three nearby things: A pipeline. A deployment pipeline breaks the build into stages, each adding confidence at the cost of more time 9 . A workflow often uses a pipeline to run its checks, but it also holds the agent's task, the human decision and the evidence left behind, none of which a pipeline owns. A process. A documented process says how work ought to go. A workflow exists only when it runs and leaves evidence each time; a procedure that nobody follows is not one. A prompt. A prompt asks the agent to behave in a certain way; it enforces nothing. Inside a workflow, a prompt is at most one part of the agent's task, and every rule that must hold is enforced by a check or decided by a person. Why it matters AI assistance can raise the volume of change without raising a team's capacity to judge it. DORA's 2024 research estimated that, as AI adoption increased, software delivery throughput and stability both fell, and it pointed teams back to basics such as small batch sizes and robust testing 3 . Its 2025 report, State of AI-assisted Software Development , found AI adoption now goes with higher throughput but still with lower delivery stability, describes AI as an amplifier of a team's existing strengths and weaknesses, and names strong automated testing, mature version control practices and fast feedback loops as the control systems that stop a rise in change volume from turning into instability 4 . Those control systems need a place to attach. Without a defined workflow, a change advances on a status flag or a conversation, and a month later the team cannot reconstruct which checks ran or whose call it was. Agent output is accepted on trust, reviewers spend their time on things a tool could catch, and a failed check gets waved through or fixed off the record, so it fails the same way next time. A workflow is the recommended answer: the smallest unit to which a team can attach checks, a named decision and a record, and then improve from what that record shows. This is presented as recommended practice; no public study measures the effect of defining work this way. How it works The parts of a workflow definition The table gives each part, what it holds, and how it reads for one running example: verifying a pull request for the customer-record export , a feature that lets users export customer records (the pull-request verification entry in the workflow catalog ). Part What it holds In the export example Trigger The event that starts a run A pull request is marked ready, or its revision changes Inputs Upstream records and the rules that apply The readiness record for the export specification; rules R-042 (who may export which records) and R-017 (the volume limit for large exports) Agent task What the agent does, inside set limits A review skill reads the diff against the specification and the two rules and writes findings tagged to rule identifiers Checks Deterministic checks the change's risk tier selects The R-042 access validator and the R-017 load scenario Guardrails What the agent may and may not touch The agent can comment on the pull request; it cannot approve, merge or change the checks Human decision The named person who decides, and on what The reviewer decides whether the change is ready; the security owner decides on anything touching R-042 Outputs The evidence record the run leaves Each check with its result, the agent's findings and how each was resolved, and the decisions, tied to the revision Feedback Where a miss is classified and sent A defect found later is traced back to this run and becomes a new test or a sharper rule Owner One person accountable for the workflow itself The engineering lead who owns merge readiness The inputs matter as much as the checks. When an agent writes both the code and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both can share one mistaken assumption, so verification needs an independent basis defined apart from the implementation: here, the readiness record and the two rules. Spec-driven toolkits produce that kind of upstream input by turning requirements into a specification, a plan and tasks before implementation starts 22 . A run is worth starting only if it can reach a decision. As recommended practice, the workflow first confirms that the records it reads exist and are current, and that the change is small enough to examine in full. When something is missing, the run stops and states what it is waiting for, rather than working around the gap. Size matters more once an agent writes the code: a broader request yields more code, more tests and more prose, while the time a reviewer can give does not grow to match. Keeping each change within what one reviewer can read in full is recommended practice rather than a measured finding. It applies, at the scale of one change, the advice DORA gives when it lists working in small batches among the capabilities that amplify the benefit of AI 5 . The three roles: agent, checks and people Every workflow splits its work three ways and keeps the three apart. The agent takes on high-volume work where an imperfect first attempt is cheap to correct, such as searching the codebase, writing code and tests, and summarising a diff for review. Its output feeds a decision someone else makes. The checks enforce what a tool can decide reliably and what must not be wrong. Böckeler separates computational controls, which are deterministic and fast (tests, linters, type checkers), from inferential ones such as AI code review, which are more expensive and non-deterministic but give richer semantic judgment 1 . On this site, a deterministic check tied to a rule identifier is a validator, and an agent that reads a diff and proposes findings is a review skill 2 . The review skill informs a decision; it never stands in for a check that must not be wrong. The people make the calls that depend on context the workflow cannot hold, from accepting a specification to letting a change ship; each call is recorded under the name of whoever made it. One model vendor's account of an agent-first team describes the same split as people steering while agents execute, with constraints enforced by automated checks 19 . Risk frameworks expect it too: the NIST AI Risk Management Framework calls for policies and procedures that define and differentiate roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and the oversight of AI systems 18 . The agent's limits come from the permissions of the identity it runs under, not from its instructions. In the export example, the review skill's credential can post comments on the pull request but holds no merge right and no write access to the check configuration, so no wording in a prompt can widen what it does. This is least privilege, which NIST's control catalogue applies to processes acting on behalf of users as well as to the users themselves 16 . Blurring the roles fails in two ways: The agent treated as verifier. NIST's profile for generative AI lists over-reliance and automation bias among the risks of human-AI configuration 17 . A widely cited review of the research reports that people relying on an imperfect decision aid both miss what it misses and follow it when it is wrong, that experts and novices are affected alike, and that training or instructions alone do not prevent it 20 . In one user study, participants with an AI code assistant wrote less secure code than those without one, yet were more likely to believe their code was secure 21 . So AI review can raise findings but never grants approval. People treated as checks. Reviewers re-check formatting, test coverage or rule compliance that a tool could enforce, and their attention runs out before the real decisions. Each such rule moves to a gate. What keeps the roles apart is that no party both produces a result and accepts it, the idea security controls call separation of duties 16 . The agent that wrote the export code does not decide whether it satisfies R-042: the validator does, and the security owner decides on the access design. Risk tiers: same definition, different cost A risk tier is a label, set when the change is planned, that decides which checks and which reviewers a run requires; the workflow's definition stays the same at every tier. Scaling verification effort to risk is established testing practice: in risk-based testing, the type and level of risk govern which test activities are selected and how much effort they receive 13 12 . As recommended practice, the tier follows from what the change touches, such as the data it reads and the rules that apply, and a lower tier never drops a rule that applies. In the export example, the change reads customer data and applies an access rule, so its tier calls for both the R-042 validator and the R-017 load scenario, and adds the owner of the access rule as a required reviewer. A change to the export button's label would run the same workflow with fewer checks and one reviewer. The tier set at planning can turn out wrong once the diff exists, so the recommended practice is to work it out again for each revision. If a revision of the label change also edits the export query, the tier rises and the R-042 validator and the security owner join the run. Failure paths A failure path is the defined response to one kind of interruption. Each names who acts next, and the fix is made where the problem started, not where it was noticed. In the export example: A check finds a violation. The R-042 validator fails because a background export job reads records the requesting user may not see. The change goes back to implementation, is fixed and the check reruns. A required check could not run. The R-017 load scenario reports could_not_run because the load-test tool is missing from the runner image. The run cannot show a positive status, and the runner image's owner is told. The result is neither a pass nor a defect in the code; the fix belongs to whoever maintains the runner. A requirement is ambiguous. The review skill notes that the specification does not say whether deleted customers are exported. The specification's owner answers and the specification is updated; nobody settles it in code. An agent finding is rejected. The reviewer rejects a finding as a false alarm. The rejection and its reason are recorded, so the review skill can be tuned against real misses. An exception is requested. The change would let one export go past R-017's row limit. The request goes to whoever holds that decision right, and a granted exception is recorded against R-017 with an owner, a reason and an expiry. R-042, as an access rule, is not open to exception. Treating a check that produced no result as a pass is the most damaging mistake on this list, because a broken check then passes every change it was meant to stop. As recommended practice, only an explicit pass counts as a pass. A check that times out, crashes or never reports is shown as a state of its own, so the run cannot show a positive status; what that means for the merge is set in assurance. Continuous integration practice already treats a broken build as something to fix at once rather than wave through 8 . Each return also says where the problem started, and as recommended practice the record keeps that cause. A string of could_not_run results traced to one runner image is a platform fix, not a coding one, and the workflow's owner can see that only if returns are recorded by cause. What a workflow hands on What a workflow produces is a record that later steps can read, rather than a notification that something is done. The next workflow consults that record; it does not run the checks again or ask around: the readiness record configures verification, and the verification record for the export change is what release readiness later reads. This evidence hand-off only works if each record names the exact revision it describes. A new revision gets a new record and the old one stays as history, since a result for an earlier revision says nothing reliable about the code as it is now. The fields a record holds are fixed by the Evidence schema . Findings also travel backward. When a defect reaches users, the team works out which workflow should have caught it and why it did not, and that workflow's owner receives the finding. This is the feedback path , the site's name for what Böckeler calls the steering loop 1 . When a team has a workflow As recommended practice, a team has a workflow once every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record the next decision reads: for the export feature, anyone can open the verification record for the pull request's latest revision and see what ran and who decided. Whether the workflow improves delivery then shows in the team's software delivery performance measures 6 . The list of workflows across the lifecycle, each with its decision, trigger, agent task, checks, human decision and evidence, is the workflow catalog . Where it sits on the map Workflows sit in the core band, the part of the map that shows what does the work. The band reads as one row: Harness engineering, then the Engineering Kit , then Workflows, then the Software factory. Before workflows comes Harness engineering , the discipline of deciding what an agent may read and do, what a machine checks and what a person decides. Next, still before workflows, is the Engineering Kit , the installable package every workflow draws on: its Rule registry supplies the rules a run applies, its Validators are the checks, its Skills with evals shape the agent's task, and its Evidence schema fixes what each run records. After workflows comes the Software factory , the operating state that appears when many workflows share rules, evidence and feedback. Outside the core band, the lifecycle band places each workflow in its phase, through the workflow catalog . The assurance band reads the evidence records a workflow leaves, and the adoption path decides which workflow a team builds first. Pitfalls A documented process mistaken for a workflow. The steps are written down but runs leave no record. Sign: nobody can show the evidence record for last week's changes. The agent as approver. An AI review comment is read as sign-off. Sign: reviewers approve within minutes of the agent's summary, with no findings of their own. Reviewers doing a tool's job. Review threads fill with comments about formatting, missing tests or naming rules. Sign: the same kind of comment recurs across many changes; each one is a rule waiting to become a gate. Silence read as success. A required check is missing from the results and the change merges anyway. Sign: the list of expected checks is not recorded before results arrive. The documentation of at least one widely used change host states that a job skipped because of a condition reports its status as success 11 , so a check that never ran can look like a pass unless it is reported as its own state. A flaky check re-run until it passes. The pass after a retry is recorded like any other, and the check stops meaning anything. Sign: one check fails and passes on the same revision with no change in between. Non-deterministic tests erode trust in the whole suite, and quarantine is at most a short-term, bounded measure while the cause is fixed 10 . Exceptions that never end. The same waiver is granted change after change. Sign: exceptions with no expiry date, or one rule collecting most of the exceptions. A run too large to review. More is attempted in one change than a reviewer can read with care. Sign: time spent reviewing does not grow with change size, or large diffs are approved with few comments. The fix is to split the work before it starts. Tiers chosen for convenience. A change is put in a lighter tier to save time. Sign: the recorded tier does not match what the change touched, or a lighter tier carries no reason and no name. Hand-off by conversation. The next workflow asks in chat whether security looked at the change. Sign: a downstream decision cites a message rather than an evidence record. Related Harness engineering : the discipline a workflow puts into practice. Engineering Kit : the reusable package every workflow draws on. Rule registry : where the rules a workflow applies, and their owners, are kept. Validators : the deterministic checks, and how they report a result that could not be produced. Skills with evals : the packaged guidance behind the agent's task and the review skill. Evidence schema : the fixed shape of the record each run leaves. Software factory : what emerges when many workflows share rules, evidence and feedback. Workflow catalog : the list of workflows across the lifecycle, including pull-request verification . Workflow in the terminology : the short definition and its attribution. Sources Lean value-stream practice: the Lean Enterprise Institute's definitions of value-stream mapping 15 and the value-stream manager 14 , and DORA's guide to value stream mapping 7 . Pipelines, continuous integration and test reliability: Martin Fowler on the deployment pipeline 9 , continuous integration 8 and non-deterministic tests 10 . AI-assisted delivery: DORA's 2024 findings 3 , its 2025 report 4 , its AI Capabilities Model 5 and its research programme 6 . Harness vocabulary: Birgitta Böckeler on harness engineering 1 and on sensors 2 , and one model vendor's account of harness engineering in an agent-first team 19 . Human oversight and over-reliance: the NIST AI Risk Management Framework 18 , its generative AI profile 17 , Parasuraman and Manzey's review of automation bias 20 and Perry and colleagues' study of AI code assistants 21 . Separation of duties and least privilege: NIST's security and privacy control catalogue 16 . Risk-based testing: the ISTQB glossary 13 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-1 12 . Upstream inputs and result states: an open-source spec-driven toolkit 22 and one change host's documentation on skipped checks 11 . The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. On this site, an architecture rule expressed as a fitness function that runs with the build is a validator, and an architecture gate once it blocks. adopted ford-evolutionary-architectures Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a verify command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a few validators for rules the team has broken before, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency rules, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. It proposes; it cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Flexible and scalable, but itself non-deterministic and subject to position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so its grades are checked against human judgement before they are relied on. In an eval set it is one kind of grader, alongside code-based checks and human review. adopted zheng-llm-judge Evidence record What a run records in one fixed shape, as a by-product of the run rather than a report written afterwards: schema version, change and configuration revisions, kit version, the checks expected before the run, each check's result with its rule ID, status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending and taken, and an overall status derived from the rest. Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable), it timed out again after one retry, or the tool itself crashed. It is never reported as passed or skipped; what it means for a merge or release is decided in assurance. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. The name is this site's; the distinction is established, for example in SARIF's record of whether a tool's execution succeeded, and in test frameworks that report errors apart from failures. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives), a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended), a work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. It translates; it holds no rules, validator logic or schema. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. The Engineering Kit's tool adapters apply the same idea to the tools a kit runs against. adopted cockburn-hexagonal Anticorruption layer Eric Evans's domain-driven design pattern: an isolating layer that talks to another system through its existing interface and translates between the two models, so the other system's concepts do not reshape the model that uses it. It runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes. On this site, the contract suite a kit's core defines for each kind of adapter is the same idea pointed at the kit's own interface. adopted fowler-contract-test Consumer-driven contract Ian Robinson's service-evolution pattern: the consumers of a service state their expectations as tests, and the provider is checked against all of them, so it can change without breaking any consumer. adopted robinson-cdc Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. The idea of scaling test effort to risk comes from risk-based testing. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating state that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. Coined in this sense. Earlier uses of the phrase mean something else: Cusumano (1991) for Japanese firms that applied production-management discipline to large-scale software development, and Greenfield and Short (2004) for model-driven production of variants of a standard product. Recent writing on the "dark software factory", where agents produce software that no person reviews, is not what is meant either, nor is the industrial sense of identical outputs from a fixed process. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, plan and tasks, with clarification added where the specification leaves questions open. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. The law does not say fewer controls are better. This site's recommendation follows from shrinking what is governed: narrow what the agent may produce first, on a few well-defined execution surfaces, then start with a small set of controls fitted to failures actually seen. adopted ashby
